clue.text: Novel that's winning

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Jane Austen's last completed novel
second meaning: the act of winning someone over to a view

explanation.surface: A reviewer praises a book as a winner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winning' looks like an adjective praising the novel, but it is a noun here: the winning over of someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen titled a novel with this word, and it also names the act of bringing someone round by argument.

clue.text: Puts cushions in frogs' homes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fills with soft stuffing, as in padding a chair
second meaning: the lily leaves frogs sit on

explanation.surface: Someone furnishes frog houses with soft cushions.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means adds soft stuffing; the noun names floating lily leaves, where cartoon frogs live, and slang for one's home.

clue.text: Groomsmen regularly downed wine

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so only every other letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the word

explanation.surface: At a wedding, the groomsmen kept knocking back the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downed' reads as drinking in the surface; cryptically it only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosé is a pink wine, written in crosswords without its accent.

clue.text: Going to disturb nun during nap

indicators.note: disturbing things knocks them out of place, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: all twelve letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone sets off to wake a dozing nun.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of the three words gives UP AND RUNNING.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up and running is operating, working properly, functioning: in that sense it is going.

clue.text: Ferociously, ambitiously, a boy strangely wanting encouragement

definitions.note: a plural noun defined by a mass noun

indicators.note: strangely says the letters to be removed may appear in any order
doing something ferociously means violently, so the word is wildly rearranged
wanting means lacking, so the letters named after it are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these four letters come out

explanation.surface: A string of adverbs describing a boy who is hungry for praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A, B, O, Y from AMBITIOUSLY, leaving MITIUSL, and rearrange to STIMULI.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimuli are spurs or incentives that rouse activity, which is what encouragement provides.

clue.text: Ill — almost ill — it's when there's less activity

indicators.note: almost means not quite, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: feeling off means feeling unwell
peaky is British slang for pale and unwell

explanation.surface: Someone describes feeling poorly and when the quiet times are.
explanation.walkthrough: Peaky is everyday British for looking pale and sickly; cut short it becomes PEAK.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-peak hours are the quieter times when travel, phone lines or power use see lower demand.

clue.text: So shut up

indicators.note: things that are up are disturbed or amiss, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' reads as a command to be quiet; 'up' alone is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean therefore or in this way, as in 'thus it was settled'.

clue.text: Drunk chairman's admitted love for noises in Dylan records

indicators.note: to be admitted is to be let inside, so one piece goes within the other
a drunk person is all over the place, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, the S included
love is nil in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A tipsy chairman confesses a fondness for Bob Dylan's records.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan famously plays mouth organs on a neck rack, so their wailing sound is all over his albums.

clue.text: Loins dimly aroused by position

indicators.note: aroused means stirred up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A racy line about loins faintly stirred by a sexual position.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the bedroom; the position is on a cricket field. Silly mid-on is a fielder standing very close to the batter on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, fielders occupy named places, and this is one of them, perilously near the bat.

clue.text: Put out novel, Daisy's Fist

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A book called Daisy's Fist is published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like publishing the novel, and 'novel' looks like a book; both are false.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone out is to annoy or disappoint them, which is to leave them unsatisfied.

clue.text: Spoken of the country? Not once

indicators.note: not having something means it is absent, so that word is taken off

parts.note: pastoral describes rural life and the countryside
once means formerly, in the past

explanation.surface: A question about whether a dialect belongs to the nation, with a curt reply.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral exam or agreement is done by mouth rather than in writing.

clue.text: Unprincipled, odd, tiny and drawn out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of some strange, small, haggard figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn out' looks like a phrase meaning prolonged; 'out' alone is the anagram signal, and 'and' just joins the fodder words.
explanation.definitionFit: Down-and-dirty tactics are ruthless and unscrupulous, ignoring rules of fair play.

clue.text: Book where one more duty laid out?

indicators.note: laid out means set out in a fresh arrangement, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A book in which yet another obligation is set down.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting, since Deuteronomy restates the law, laying out duty upon duty for the Israelites.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the fifth book of the Old Testament, one of the five books of Moses.

clue.text: Since university, gets into reading? Typical

parts.note: as in 'as it was raining' means since

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a perusal is a careful read
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Since starting university, someone has got into books, which is only to be expected.
explanation.walkthrough: The university's U slips into the middle of the reading word, after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens as per usual follows the normal pattern, so it is typical of how things go.

clue.text: 20 to go on here?

parts.note: a score is twenty
to board a bus or ship is to go on it

explanation.surface: A player needs twenty more points to win, and wonders where they will be posted.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' looks like a cross-reference to 20-across, but it is just the number twenty. The whole clue also describes where a score of 20 is posted at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket or football ground shows the running totals on a large display panel, so a score like 20 goes up there.

clue.text: Primarily, some uncanny carnal creatures undertaking bedroom incursions?

definitions.text: some uncanny carnal creatures undertaking bedroom incursions?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each following word is taken

parts.words: some uncanny carnal creatures undertaking bedroom incursions
parts.note: the initial letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A description of eerie lustful spirits that invade bedrooms at night.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore these are female demons who visit sleeping men to seduce them, exactly the night visitors described.

clue.text: Twice king and I eat, on time for expedition

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the first pair swallows the next letters

parts.note: K for king and I as written, the pair repeated
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone eats with a king, twice, punctually, before setting off on an expedition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' applies to the pair king-and-I; only the first copy does the eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 raft voyage across the Pacific from Peru to Polynesia bore this name.

clue.text: Commissions whereby queen's collecting money in S Africa

indicators.note: collecting means gathering in, so the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, plus the S of the possessive
the rand is South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: A queen is paid in South African currency for her work.
explanation.definitionFit: Errands are small tasks one is sent to do for someone, which is what commissions in this sense are.

clue.text: Cover that woman to keep warmth in

indicators.note: keeping something means holding on to it, so one piece holds the other
in completes keep in, confirming the second piece goes inside

parts.note: a pronoun for a woman already mentioned
heat is warmth

explanation.surface: Wrap her up so she doesn't lose heat.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a blade in its scabbard or to encase something protectively is to cover it.

clue.text: Old desire with eagerness cut short

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to long for is to desire
agog means full of eager excitement

explanation.surface: An elderly person's impatient wishes are thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: AGOG with its final G removed leaves AGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Things from a remote time in history are ancient, and the phrase describes that distant past.

clue.text: Drained and percolated audibly

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the word is taken by its sound alone

parts.note: liquid that has leached has seeped slowly through

explanation.surface: Coffee filtered through a strainer and was drained.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeches suck blood, so something leeched has had its life or resources sucked out, exhausted and drained.

clue.text: Pope with explanatory note for piece of Apocrypha…?

parts.note: Urban is the name of several popes
the key explaining symbols on a map

explanation.surface: A pope annotates a passage of the biblical Apocrypha.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apocrypha' looks biblical, but here it means stories of doubtful truth, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocryphal tales are widely told but unverified, and an urban legend is a modern story of exactly that kind.

clue.text: Bit of tsarina's dress

indicators.note: a bit of something is a part of it, so the letters sit inside the next word

parts.note: the second to fifth letters of this word

explanation.surface: A scrap of a Russian empress's gown.
explanation.definitionFit: This long draped garment is the traditional dress of women in South Asia.

clue.text: Reportedly 'breaks down stains'

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the word is taken by how it is spoken

parts.note: a machine that dies has broken down

explanation.surface: A quoted claim that something gets rid of stains.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like a product's advertising boast.
explanation.definitionFit: To colour fabric with a pigment is to stain or tint it, so the verbs coincide.

clue.text: Headgear, uniform back-to-front in western state

indicators.note: back-to-front means the wrong way round, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: a hat is headgear
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A cap worn backwards with a uniform out West.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a US state in the Rocky Mountain region of the American West, capital Salt Lake City.

clue.text: Set apart, gutted, they bypass study

indicators.note: a gutted thing has had its insides removed, so only the outer letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

indicators.note: to bypass is to go round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: taken as written
to read a subject at university is to study it

explanation.surface: Someone apart and devastated finds others skipping the study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, but here it means emptied, and 'bypass' means going round.
explanation.definitionFit: Being prepared and poised for immediate action is what both mean, as in 'ready, steady, go'.

clue.text: Some dilly-dallying reactionary peer

indicators.note: a reactionary wants to go backwards, so the letters run from right to left
some means a portion, so the letters are a run within the words that follow

parts.note: the last letter of the first part and three of the second

explanation.surface: A conservative member of the House of Lords who dithers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a peeress or a woman holding a title is addressed with this rank, so she belongs to the peerage.

clue.text: Listen up: Everyman's in peril, sad, quivering

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other
quivering means shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the setter speaking of something of theirs says my

explanation.surface: A frightened, tearful setter trembles in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for the setter, so Everyman's means my.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic demands that someone pay close attention, the second made famous by George H. W. Bush.
